title: Psalms of Solomon
subtitle: eighteen psalms from Jerusalem after Pompey, and a prayer for the son of David
lead: The Psalms of Solomon are eighteen Jewish psalms, first written in Hebrew and kept only in Greek and in a Syriac translation. They come from Jerusalem in the years after 63 BC, when the Roman general Pompey broke into the Temple mount, walked into the Temple and took captives to Rome. The poems grieve that disaster and explain it: God let a foreign conqueror in because Jerusalem's own leaders had sinned in secret and defiled the holy things (1; 2; 8). Psalm 2 reaches its climax with the proud conqueror, "the dragon" (2:29), pierced on the mountains of Egypt and his body carried on the waves with no one to bury him (2:30–31), as Pompey was killed on the Egyptian shore in 48 BC. Between these poems come the prayers of a group that calls itself the devout: they accept God's discipline as a father's, trust his mercy to the poor, and expect the sinners to perish while those who fear the Lord rise to eternal life (3:16). Psalms 17 and 18 pray for a king of David's line, the son of David (17:23), who will drive the nations and the law-breakers out of Jerusalem, gather a holy people, and rule by the word of his mouth. The book has 18 psalms and 332 verses, with headings on every psalm but the first.

In no church's Bible. No church counts the Psalms of Solomon as Scripture, and no Jewish source names them: every ancient witness that Ryle and James collected is Christian, and Jongkind finds the book "only within Christian transmission." They survived because Christians copied them, most often between Wisdom and Sirach. The oldest witness is the table of contents of Codex Alexandrinus (400s AD), which lists the book after its count of the books of both Testaments. "If the Codex itself contained these Psalms," Swete wrote, "they have perished together with a portion" of 2 Clement, the book listed just before them. Greek canon lists put it among the disputed books or the apocrypha. This site reads it as historians and theologians read it: as a rare dated window on Jewish faith and politics in the generation before Jesus, and above all on the hope for a Messiah that the Gospels share and also change.

Why it matters. Few Jewish writings can be dated so closely, and none outside the Bible gives so full a picture of a coming son of David. Its words for him, its "sinners" and "devout," its hope that the scattered tribes will be gathered and its trust in God's mercy stand close to the world of Luke 1–2. Read it beside Psalm 2, Psalm 72, Isaiah 11 and the Gospels, and weigh it by them.
facts: No church. It is not in the Old Testament of the Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican or Protestant churches, and not in the Hebrew Bible. The table of contents of Codex Alexandrinus lists it after its count of the biblical books; the Pseudo-Athanasian Synopsis and the Stichometry of Nicephorus list it among the disputed books, and the list of the Sixty Books, attached to the Questions and Answers of Anastasius Sinaita, among the apocrypha (Swete; Gray).

Unknown. The headings say "of Solomon," but the headings of single psalms are generally thought to be later than the psalms (Atkinson). One writer, or several of one generation (Gray), from a strict, devout circle in Jerusalem: the Pharisees in the classic and still commonest view (Ryle and James; Gray; Swete; Toy; Reid; Chai), the Essenes for A. Dupont-Sommer, and for J. O'Dell, J. H. Charlesworth, K. Atkinson and U. Chai a group that cannot be tied to any party known by name (Chai; Atkinson).

Mostly between 63 BC, when Pompey took Jerusalem, and the 40s BC. Psalm 2 was written after Pompey's death in 48 BC (Gray; Toy). Ryle and James set 70 and 40 BC as the outer limits; Toy suggested about 45 BC. Some date Psalm 17 a little later, to the Parthian invasion of 40 BC (J. Tromp) or to the siege by Herod and Sosius in 37 BC (K. Atkinson), as Jongkind reports. The Temple still stands, so VanderKam thinks it "likely" that the book was written before AD 70, though its date "cannot be determined precisely."

Jerusalem and Judea under the last Hasmonean rulers and in the first years of Roman control: the quarrel of the brothers Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, Pompey's siege of the Temple mount in 63 BC, the slaughter there, and the captives taken to the west.

Psalms, shaped on the biblical Psalter: laments for Jerusalem (1; 2; 8), wisdom psalms on the righteous and the sinner (3; 13; 14; 15), a curse on a hypocrite (4), prayers and thanksgivings (5; 6; 7; 9; 10; 12; 16), a song of return (11), and two royal psalms for the coming king (17; 18).

Written in Hebrew, in the common view (Gray; Toy; Schürer); kept in Greek, and in a Syriac version that most scholars think was made from the Greek (Gray; Atkinson), though some argue it was made from the Hebrew (Trafton, Ward, as Jongkind reports). No Hebrew copy survives.

18 psalms, 332 verses, with headings (verse 0 on this site) on Psalms 2–18. The site numbers the verses as Swete does; most modern books use Rahlfs's numbers, and only Psalms 1 and 16 come out the same, apart from 16:2 (see "Three ways of numbering").

The Greek printed by H. B. Swete, The Old Testament in Greek, vol. 3: a text taken from a collation of Codex Romanus (Vatican Greek 336, Swete's r) and corrected in places from von Gebhardt's edition, with the readings of seven other manuscripts in the notes (Swete, vol. 3, introduction).
authorship: The headings put "Of Solomon" over Psalms 2–18, as the site's Psalm 72:0 and Psalm 127:0 read "Of Solomon." Christian copies and lists call the book "Psalms of Solomon," and three Greek manuscripts call it "Wisdom of Solomon" (Jongkind). The title, Atkinson writes, "ascribes the collection to King Salomon"; the lists that name the book treat it as disputed or apocryphal. Reid says the collection itself "makes no pretensions to authorship by Solomon" and that "the name of the wise king became associated with it later." Jongkind leaves open whether the psalms were written in Solomon's name or the name was attached later, "for example at the occasion of the translation." Atkinson (NETS) thinks the name came from the son of David in 17:23, which some scribe took to mean Solomon. Toy thought a later psalm book would naturally go under the name of Solomon, who stood next to David in fame as a writer and is named in the headings of two biblical psalms.

Ryle and James (1891) titled their edition Psalms of the Pharisees. With Gray (1913) they argued that the book's righteous and devout are the Pharisees, and its sinners the Sadducee nobles and the Hasmonean house: the sinners run the Temple service and profane it (1:8; 2:3; 8:12; 8:26) and set up a kingdom not of David's line (17:6–8), while the devout keep the Law with care, atone for sins of ignorance (3:8–9), take suffering as discipline, hope for the son of David and expect to rise to life. Ryle and James wrote that in these lines "a Pharisee assails the Asmonean house." Swete, Toy and the Catholic Encyclopedia agreed; Swete called the psalms "the work of the Pharisaic school," and Reid (1907) called it the view on which scholars were "commonly agreed." In 2011 Unha Chai could still write that "it is still the Pharisees that the righteous have been most commonly identified with," though he doubts it: the Pharisees were not political quietists like the psalms' righteous, and there is little evidence that they held the hope for a Davidic Messiah.

Soon after the Dead Sea Scrolls were found, A. Dupont-Sommer argued that the righteous of the psalms belonged to the Qumran community, and so were Essenes. P. Franklyn and R. Hann found real links with the Scrolls (both groups recall exile from Jerusalem and attack illegitimate religious rulers and their wealth), but not enough to settle who wrote the psalms (all as summarized by Chai, 2011). Jongkind (2002) notes that since the Scrolls were found the Pharisee identification "is seen as less secure."
A group we cannot name, and other proposals

J. O'Dell (1961) argued that the marks usually taken as Pharisaic belonged to "the general eschatologically-minded population," and Charlesworth finds no convincing evidence linking the psalms to a defined sect (both as summarized by Chai, 2011). Atkinson's 1998 article on their date speaks of them as the work of "an Unknown Jewish Sect." Chai (2011) concludes that, since many groups of the time are lost to us, the righteous "have to remain a religious group otherwise unknown and shadowy to us." Other proposals: the heirs of the Hasidim (A. Büchler; D. Flusser) and Zadokite priests pushed out of the Temple (H. Kim) (all as summarized by Chai).

Gray found one tone throughout and judged the psalms the work, "if not of a single hand, yet of a single generation." Ryle and James thought Psalms 4 and 12, where the sinners are cursed but not yet punished, might be the oldest, written before Pompey came (as Gray reports). Jongkind thinks Psalm 11, a song of return, may not share the others' date.

audience.to: The devout of Jerusalem and Judea in the generation after 63 BC. They called themselves the devout, the righteous, those who fear the Lord and the poor. They had watched two Hasmonean brothers fight over the throne and the high priesthood, then seen a Roman army breach the Temple walls, kill thousands and carry captives to the west (Josephus, Antiquities 14.4, sections 14.54–79). The book speaks of the assemblies of the devout (17:18), and its headings and Selah marks (17:31; 18:10) suggest psalms meant for prayer and singing together. Soon the poems were read in Greek, which is most often dated to the first century AD (Jongkind), and later Christians copied them.
audience.why: To make sense of disaster and to keep hope alive. The psalms tell the devout that God is just: Jerusalem fell because its rulers sinned in secret (1; 8), and the proud conqueror fell in his turn (2). They tell them to take their suffering as a father's discipline and to keep the Law (3; 10; 13; 14), that God still feeds the poor and hears the one who calls on him (5; 6; 15), and that the sinners will perish while those who fear the Lord will live. Above all they hold God to his oath to David (17:5): God will raise up a son of David to clear Jerusalem of foreigners and law-breakers and to rule in holiness. Knowing the readers changes the reading. The "sinners" are often not pagans but other Jews, the ruling party, so the curses of Psalm 4 and the anger of Psalm 17 are the words of people out of power. Their hope for the Messiah is the hope of people with no king of their own, no army and no say in the Temple.
views: Ryle and James, Gray and Toy: Pharisees writing against the Sadducee nobles and the Hasmonean kings, soon after Pompey's conquest.

O'Dell, Charlesworth, Atkinson and Chai: a devout group that cannot be tied to any party known by name; Dupont-Sommer: the Essenes. Either way the readers are the people the psalms call the devout and the poor (Chai).

The Greek translation was made before AD 70 in the view of Ryle and James, and also of Viteau, who disagreed with them on Baruch (as Gray reports); for Jews abroad the poems' history was still recent and clear (Jongkind).

outline: The alarm of war: Jerusalem thought herself righteous, but her children sinned in secret
About Jerusalem: the battering ram and the altar trampled, Jerusalem stripped of her glory, the dragon's death in Egypt, the just Judge praised
About the righteous: the righteous accept discipline and rise to life, the sinner falls and does not rise
To the people-pleasers: the hypocrite in the council, a curse on his house, a blessing on those who fear the Lord
God feeds the poor and every living thing; enough with righteousness is better than too much
Happy the one who calls on the name of the Lord
Do not move your dwelling from us: discipline us yourself, not by the nations
War at Jerusalem: the hidden sins, the cup of wine, the rulers who open the gates, the slaughter; God shown just; a prayer to gather the scattered
Israel led into exile; God the just Judge; our works are in the choice of our soul; mercy for those who confess
Happy the one whom the Lord disciplines
The trumpet in Zion: Jerusalem's children gathered from east and west
The righteous spared: their discipline is not like the sinner's ruin
The devout live by the Law; the sinners inherit Hades
God's sign on the righteous, the mark of destruction on the sinners
The soul that nearly slipped, and God who held it back
The kingdom of God; the usurpers of David's throne and the foreign man; the prayer for the son of David and his reign
The day of mercy and the Lord's Messiah; the lights of heaven keep their course

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars read the Psalms of Solomon as poems of a devout Jerusalem circle written between Pompey's conquest (63 BC) and the 40s BC, translated from a lost Hebrew original into Greek; the lens asks what events lie behind each psalm, which party wrote it, and how the Greek and its few late manuscripts preserve it.

lenses.name: Jewish setting
lenses.desc: The book as a Jewish document of the late Second Temple: the devout against the sinners, the Temple and its priests, the Law kept with care, the hopes of Jews under the Hasmoneans and Rome. Judaism did not keep it, and the lens also asks why.

lenses.name: New Testament background
lenses.desc: Readers who study the world of Jesus: the son of David and the Messiah, "sinners" as a party word, the Pharisees, the hope of Israel's restoration and the gathering of the tribes, and the many shared phrases with Luke 1–2, without claiming that the New Testament quotes the book.

lenses.name: The Psalter's patterns
lenses.desc: How these poems use the forms and phrases of the biblical Psalms: lament, thanksgiving, wisdom and curse psalms, the headings and Selah, and above all the royal theology of Psalms 2, 72 and 89 and God's oath to David.

lenses.name: Christian reception: read, not Scripture
lenses.desc: Christians copied the book beside Wisdom and Sirach, the table of contents of Codex Alexandrinus lists it after its biblical books, and the canon lists set it among the disputed books; no church counts it as Scripture. The lens reads it as a Christian reader can today, as a witness to the hope that Jesus fulfilled and also changed, tested against the Bible.

sections.b:
The Plain English Translation is made for this site from the Greek as printed by H. B. Swete in The Old Testament in Greek, volume 3. Swete took his text from a collation of one manuscript, Codex Romanus (Vatican Greek 336, which he calls r), corrected in places from Oscar von Gebhardt's edition of 1895, and gave the readings of seven other manuscripts in his notes (Swete, vol. 3, introduction). There is no ancient Hebrew to check it against, so where the Greek is hard the notes say how scholars explain it, often as a misread Hebrew word (Gray; Toy). Every place where the Plain English Translation departs from Swete's text has a variant note.

The headings are verse 0, as on the site's Psalms; Psalm 1 has none in Swete's text. "Of Solomon" renders the Greek tō Salōmōn, as in the site's Psalm 72:0. The English check text offered beside the Greek is the translation of G. Buchanan Gray in R. H. Charles's Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha (1913), which the site's copy calls "Charles"; its verse numbers often differ from Swete's, and the site lines it up by sense (tools/PsS-numbers.tsv).

sections.h: The name and the Solomon headings
sections.b:
Sixteen of the seventeen headings have tō Salōmōn, "of Solomon," the phrase the Greek Psalms use for the biblical Psalm 72 and Psalm 127; 4:0 has tou Salōmōn. Many add words such as "a psalm," "a hymn," "with a song" or "of the king" (17:0). The headings were probably not part of the psalms at first: Atkinson notes that the headings of single psalms "are generally thought to be secondary," vary between manuscripts, and often do not fit the psalm below them.

Why Solomon? Atkinson thinks a scribe read the son of David of 17:23 as Solomon. Toy thought a new psalm book would naturally go under the name of Solomon, second only to David as a writer of songs (1 Kings 4:32). In the manuscripts the book stands among the writings credited to Solomon, usually between Wisdom and Sirach, or after the Psalter (Swete, Introduction), and the Wisdom of Solomon offers the closest parallel: a Jewish work written centuries after Solomon in his name. Writing in a famous ancestor's name was common in this period and was not, by itself, meant to deceive.

Three psalms point to real events. A sinner breaks down the walls with a battering ram and foreign nations trample the altar (2:1–2). Jerusalem's rulers go out with joy to meet a conqueror whom God brought from the end of the earth, level the rough roads and open the gates; he seizes the towers and the wall, destroys the rulers and pours out the people's blood like unclean water (8:16–23). A lawless foreigner empties the land and sends its people as far as the west (17:13–14). The proud "dragon" is pierced on the mountains of Egypt and lies unburied on the waves (2:29–31).

Gray set these beside the accounts of Pompey. Josephus tells how the party of Hyrcanus admitted Pompey's army and handed over the city and palace while the party of Aristobulus held the Temple mount; Pompey brought battering rams from Tyre, twelve thousand Jews fell, Pompey entered the Temple and saw what only the high priest might see, and he carried Aristobulus and his children to Rome (Antiquities 14.4, sections 14.54–79). Plutarch tells how Pompey was stabbed on the shore of Egypt and his headless body left on the beach until a freedman burned it (Pompey 79–80). Gray judged that these details "in their entirety" fit no one else; Frankenberg's case for Antiochus Epiphanes had to treat the death in Egypt as a prophecy that never came true. Jongkind calls the identification with Pompey "now undisputed."

So Psalm 2 was written after 48 BC, and most of the book soon after 63 BC (Gray). Ryle and James gave 70 and 40 BC as the outer limits, Toy about 45 BC; Jongkind reports later settings proposed for Psalm 17 (40 BC, J. Tromp; 37 BC, K. Atkinson). Since the poems mourn a defiled Temple but not a destroyed one, VanderKam thinks it "likely" that they were written before AD 70, and Jongkind takes AD 70 as the latest possible date. M. de Jonge too, "although the language is traditional," sees in Psalm 2 "a reference to Pompey's death in Egypt in 48 BC." The psalms say nothing of Pompey entering the Holy of Holies, which Josephus stresses; they dwell on the trampled altar (Gray). The site's Histories of Tacitus has the Roman side: "by right of victory he went into the temple" (Histories of Tacitus 5:9).

The book divides Israel in two. On one side are the devout (hosioi, Hebrew ḥasidim), the righteous, those who fear the Lord, the poor and the innocent; on the other the sinners, the lawless and the profane, whom Psalm 4 calls people-pleasers (Gray). The sinners are rich and respectable, sit in the council, and handle the holy things (1:8; 4:1–2; 8:12). They are charged with secret sins of the body, with plundering the sanctuary and with setting up a kingship that was not David's (17:6–8). Gray notes that for these writers "alien nations are as such 'sinners'" (he cites 1:1 and 2:1–2), and the conqueror who batters down Jerusalem's walls is "the sinner" (2:1); but the sharpest words are kept for Jews.

Gray warned that this is "a strongly partisan work": neither the righteousness of the righteous nor the sins of the sinners should be taken too literally. The devout are quiet in politics. They accept suffering as God's discipline (3:4; 10:1–2; 13:7–10), atone for sins done in ignorance by fasting (3:8–9), and leave vengeance to God and his Messiah. Who they were is still argued (see "Who wrote it" above): the commonest answer is still the Pharisees (Chai), Dupont-Sommer argued for the Essenes, and O'Dell, Charlesworth, Atkinson and Chai think the group cannot be tied to any party we know.

sections.h: The Greek and the lost Hebrew
sections.b:
That the psalms were written in Hebrew is, in Gray's words, "now generally admitted." The Greek reads like a translation: it follows Hebrew word order and tense use closely, and some lines make sense only as misread Hebrew. At 2:29 the Greek has "to say the pride of the dragon," where Toy and Atkinson think the translator read a Hebrew verb for "to say" in place of one for "to change" or "turn." Atkinson notes that the translator kept to a fixed set of Greek words for Hebrew ones, so that hosios (devout) and eleos (mercy) appear again and again, even where another word would fit better. Schürer drew the conclusion that the book is Palestinian, not Alexandrian.

Ryle and James put the Greek translation "between 40 B.C. and 40 A.D.," most likely in the last decade of the first century BC; Gray sums up their case as a translation made before AD 70; Jongkind says it is most often put in the first century AD. The Syriac version is a translation of the Greek in the view of Gray and of most scholars (Atkinson), though Trafton and Ward argued that it came from the Hebrew (Jongkind).

Psalm 17 begins and ends with God as king (17:1; 17:51) and builds on God's oath to David (17:5; 2 Samuel 7:16; Psalm 89:3–4). Then it prays: look, Lord, and raise up their king, the son of David (17:23). He will shatter unjust rulers, clear Jerusalem of the nations who trample it, drive the sinners out of the inheritance and smash their pride like a potter's jars with a rod of iron (17:24–26; Psalm 2:9), and destroy law-breaking nations by the word of his mouth (17:27; Isaiah 11:4). He will gather a holy people and lead them in righteousness, judge the tribes, divide the land among them, and let no resident alien or foreigner live among them (17:28–31). The nations will serve under his yoke and come from the ends of the earth to see his glory and the glory of the Lord (17:32–35). He will not trust in horse, rider or bow, or pile up gold and silver for war (17:37; compare Psalm 20:7). He will be pure from sin (17:41), made strong in holy spirit and wise in counsel by God (17:42; Isaiah 11:2), shepherding the Lord's flock (17:45; Ezekiel 34:23). Psalm 18 calls the coming time a day of mercy and of choosing, when his Messiah comes and a generation lives under the rod of discipline of the Lord's Messiah (18:6–8).

Who is he? Toy called him "a man without supernatural power," Reid "merely human": a king raised up by God, holy and gifted, but a man of David's line. Horbury sees in him a hint of a heavenly, pre-existent Messiah (as Jongkind reports). "The Lord Messiah" (17:36). Every Greek manuscript reads christos kyrios, two titles side by side, which this site renders "the Lord Messiah." Several scholars think the Hebrew meant "the LORD's anointed" and the Greek once read christos kyriou: Rahlfs printed that correction, first proposed by A. Carrière in 1870, and Atkinson thinks a Christian scribe made the change to the nominative; Toy called it "perhaps a clerical error." The same two words stand in the Greek of Lamentations 4:20, where the Hebrew is "the LORD's anointed," and in Luke 2:11, which this site renders "He is Messiah and Lord." The heading of Psalm 18 and 18:8 have the genitive, "of the Lord's Messiah," as Simeon's "the Lord's Messiah" (Luke 2:26).

sections.h: The book and the New Testament
sections.b:
No New Testament writer quotes the Psalms of Solomon, and none names it. The links are a shared hope and shared phrases. The angel promises Mary that the Lord God will give her son "the throne of David his father" (Luke 1:32); the crowds and the blind call Jesus son of David (Matthew 9:27; Matthew 21:9); the disciples ask whether he is "giving the kingdom back to Israel" (Acts 1:6). The rod of iron of Psalm 2:9 shapes both 17:26 and Revelation 2:27 and Revelation 19:15; Isaiah 11:4 stands behind both 17:27 and 2 Thessalonians 2:8. Swete noted "interesting coincidences" between the Greek of the psalms and the Magnificat and Luke's other songs, pointing to Ryle and James, who set them out phrase by phrase. Paul's "sinners from the Gentiles" (Galatians 2:15) and the people-pleasers of Ephesians 6:6 and Colossians 3:22 use the book's words in their own way.

The differences matter as much. The son of David of Psalm 17 purges Jerusalem by driving out foreigners and sinners; Jesus eats with sinners (Mark 2:15–17) and dies for them. The Messiah here is a righteous man; the New Testament's Messiah is the Son of God who is raised from the dead (Romans 1:3–4). The book shows what many devout Jews were praying for when Jesus came, and why his kingdom surprised them.

Greek. Swete used eight manuscripts, all minuscules, dated by Swete from the 11th century (h, v) to 1419 (p); Gray puts h in the 10th or 11th: c (Casanatensis, 12th–14th century), h (Havniensis, 11th), i (Iberiticus, Mount Athos, 14th), l (Laurensis, Mount Athos, 12th), m (Mosquensis, 13th), p (Parisinus, dated 1419), r (Romanus, Vatican Greek 336, Parsons's 253: 12th century for Swete, 11th–12th for Gray and NETS) and v (Vindobonensis, 11th) (Swete, vol. 3, introduction). Gray, following von Gebhardt's study of how they descend from one lost archetype, used the same eight with capital letters. Three more have been found since Rahlfs's edition, making eleven, with no major new readings; Hann (1982) listed all their readings, and Atkinson judges manuscript 253, Swete's r, the best and earliest text (NETS). Three manuscripts call the book "Wisdom of Solomon" (Jongkind).

Syriac. A Syriac version was found by J. Rendel Harris in a manuscript that also holds the Odes of Solomon, a different work; it breaks off in Psalm 17 (Gray). Atkinson counts five Syriac manuscripts, none complete, differing from the Greek in about a tenth of the verses; W. Baars edited them for the Leiden Peshitta (1972) (NETS).

Codex Alexandrinus. The great Bible of the 400s AD opens with a list of its books. After the closing count of the books of the Old and New Testaments, and after the two letters of Clement, it adds one more: Psalms of Solomon (Swete, Introduction; Gray). Jongkind reads the entry as psalmoi Solomōntos with the number 18 (ιη΄). Swete is careful: "If the Codex itself contained these Psalms, they have perished together with a portion" of 2 Clement, the book listed just before them; in the preface to his volume 3 he says they "at one time followed the New Testament in the Codex Alexandrinus," though they are "not actually included in any uncial MS." Jongkind says only that the text "is missing from the codex." J. Rendel Harris suggested that six lost leaves of Codex Sinaiticus once held it too (Swete, Introduction).

Printed editions. The book was lost to view until the 1600s; the first edition, by J. L. de la Cerda (1626), was made from a faulty copy of the manuscript h (Gray). Ryle and James (1891), von Gebhardt (1895), Swete and Rahlfs (1935) followed.

"There is no standard versification of the Psalms of Salomon," Atkinson writes. Three systems meet on this site.

  • Swete (this site, the Greek text file, Swete's notes). Psalm 17 has 51 verses.
  • Rahlfs, which NETS follows and most modern books use. Psalm 17 has 46 verses. Only Psalms 1 and 16 keep the same numbers as Swete, apart from 16:2, which holds Rahlfs 16:1–2; elsewhere the two drift apart, by nine verses at the end of Psalm 9.
  • The English check text (Gray, in the site's copy), which is close to Swete in some psalms and to Rahlfs in others, and lacks some verses.

The verses most often cited elsewhere: Rahlfs 17:21 (the son of David) is Swete 17:23; Rahlfs 17:26–28 (the gathered tribes) is Swete 17:28–31, whose last verse runs on into Rahlfs 17:29; Rahlfs 17:32 (the Lord Messiah) is Swete 17:36; Rahlfs 9:4 (works in the choice of the soul) is Swete 9:7; Rahlfs 3:12 (rising to eternal life) is Swete 3:16; Rahlfs 2:26–27 (the death in Egypt) is Swete 2:30–31; Rahlfs 18:5 and 18:7 are Swete 18:6 and 18:8. A full table, with the English check text's numbers, is in tools/PsS-numbers.tsv.

Psalm 11 and the end of Baruch (Baruch 4:36–5:9) share a run of pictures, often in the same Greek: Jerusalem stands on a height and sees her children gathered from east and west, the high mountains are made low, the woods give shade, and God makes every fragrant tree spring up for Israel (11:3–7; Baruch 5:5–8). Who borrowed from whom?

  • Baruch borrowed from the psalm: Ryle and James, from the Greek (Swete, Introduction; Gray), and Schürer, because the psalms were first written in Hebrew. Jongkind lists R. B. Wright here too.
  • The psalm borrowed from Baruch: A. Kabasele Mukenge (as Jongkind reports).
  • Both drew on Isaiah 40 and 60 or a shared tradition: VanderKam thinks the direction "hardly obvious" and a common tradition as likely. Gray doubted Ryle and James's argument, since Baruch's poem may itself be translated from Hebrew.

The site's Baruch gives further views at Baruch 5:5. Either way, the parallel matters for dating Baruch more than for dating the psalms.

• The devout (hosioi): the group's own name, the Greek of Hebrew ḥasidim (Gray), the word behind the Hasideans of 1 Maccabees.
  • Sinners (hamartōloi): wrongdoers, and also a party label for the ruling Jews and the Gentile conqueror.
  • People-pleasers (anthrōpareskoi, 4:0): hypocrites who act for show.
  • Messiah (christos): "anointed one," the coming king of David's line.
  • Mercy (eleos): usually the Greek for ḥesed, the site's "loyal love."
  • Discipline (paideia): a father's correction of his son, the book's word for the suffering of the righteous.
  • Selah (diapsalma, 17:31; 18:10): the Greek Psalms' word for selah.
  • Pompey: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus, the Roman general who took Jerusalem in 63 BC; never named in the book.
  • Hasmoneans: the priest-kings descended from the Maccabees, whose last rulers, Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, were fighting when Pompey came.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the book answers the biblical Psalm 2
spec.body: The biblical Psalm 2 has three movements: the nations and their kings rage against the LORD and his anointed (Psalm 2:1–2); God sets his king on Zion and gives him a rod of iron to shatter them like a potter's jar (Psalm 2:6–9); and the poem ends by warning the rulers: "So then, kings, show good sense" (Psalm 2:10). My suggestion is that the collection uses this psalm as a frame. Its own Psalm 2 is the raging of a Gentile conqueror against Jerusalem, and it ends, like the biblical psalm, by turning to the rulers of the earth with the same opening, kai nyn, "and now," telling them to look at the Lord's judgment (2:36); the Greek of Psalm 2:10 also begins kai nyn. Psalm 17 then supplies the missing anointed king, with the rod of iron and the potter's jars of Psalm 2:9 (17:26). If this is right, the arrangement, not only single verses, tells the reader that the Roman disaster is the rage of Psalm 2 and the son of David is its answer. I have not found this in the scholarship I checked for this page; it rests only on the verses named.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a mirror of 1 Maccabees
spec.body: 1 Maccabees praises Simon, the first Hasmonean ruler, in the language of the prophets and royal psalms: peace in the land, each person under his own vine and fig tree (1 Maccabees 14:4–15). The Psalms of Solomon say the opposite about his heirs: they took by force what God had not promised them and laid waste the throne of David (17:6–8). My suggestion is that the two books show one argument from two sides, the Hasmonean court and its devout critics, and that the Psalms of Solomon's son of David is deliberately the kind of king the Hasmoneans could never be, since they were priests of Levi, not sons of David. The site's own notes on 1 Maccabees 14 point to the contrast; the idea that the psalms answer that royal praise on purpose is my own.

canon.summary: The Psalms of Solomon are in no church's Bible and not in the Hebrew Bible. They are eighteen Jewish psalms from the years after Pompey took Jerusalem (63 BC), kept by Christians in late Greek manuscripts and a Syriac version. The table of contents of Codex Alexandrinus lists them after its count of the books of the Bible, and the old Greek canon lists put them among the disputed books or the apocrypha.
accepted_by: Not in the Old Testament. The Orthodox Church in America names the books of its "longer canon" as Tobit, Judith, the longer Esther and Daniel, the books of Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and the Prayer of Manasseh; the Psalms of Solomon are not among them. The Stichometry of Nicephorus, patriarch of Constantinople in the early 800s, lists Psalmoi kai ōdai Solōmontos (Psalms and Odes of Solomon) among the books that antilegontai kai ouk ekklēsiazontai, that is, are disputed and not read in church, and the Pseudo-Athanasian Synopsis among the disputed books of the Old Testament (Swete, Introduction).
Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches
Not in the Old Testament. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church lists 46 Old Testament books, among them Enoch, Jubilees and the Psalms; the Psalms of Solomon are not named.

Syriac copies survive, five in all and none complete, edited by W. Baars for the Leiden edition of the Peshitta (1972) (NETS). The oldest, from the 600s, has only part of Psalm 3 as a marginal note, and in the fullest copy the eighteen psalms follow the Odes of Solomon and are numbered on from them (Jongkind; Gray). This page has no statement from the Syriac churches themselves on the book's standing.

Not Scripture. The Council of Trent's list of the sacred books (1546) does not include it. The Catholic Encyclopedia treats it among the apocryphal psalms, a work "composed in Hebrew" by a Pharisee "about the time of Pompey's capture of Jerusalem," and values it for showing the views of the Pharisees "in the age of Our Lord" (Reid, 1907).
Not Scripture, and not among the "other Books" that Article VI says the Church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners."

Not Scripture. The Westminster Confession lists the 39 books of the Hebrew Bible as the Old Testament and says that even "the books commonly called Apocrypha" are "no part of the canon of Scripture"; the Psalms of Solomon are not among those Apocrypha either.

Not Scripture, and not kept. The book is not in the Hebrew Bible and its Hebrew is lost. Toy calls it a "pseudepigraphic work not contained in the Septuagint (and therefore not included in the Apocrypha)"; that is true of the great early manuscripts, though Codex Alexandrinus lists it after its total and Swete and Rahlfs print it in their editions of the Septuagint. Every ancient reference that Ryle and James could collect is Christian.

provenance.b: The psalms were written in Hebrew, most of them soon after Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC and Psalm 2 after his death in 48 BC (Gray; Toy; Jongkind). Their Hebrew style, the Temple at the center and the parties they attack all point to Jerusalem (Schürer; Gray). Whether one poet wrote them or a circle of the devout, they come from one generation (Gray), and the eighteen seem to have traveled together as one book from early on (Jongkind).

A translator put them into a stiff, literal Greek: between 40 BC and AD 40 for Ryle and James, before AD 70 in Gray's summary of their case, and most often dated to the first century AD (Jongkind). A Syriac version followed, made from the Greek in the view of most scholars (Atkinson). The Syriac copies join the eighteen psalms to the Odes of Solomon, a different collection, and number them on from the Odes (Jongkind; Gray).

Only Christians copied the book (Jongkind). Swete's eight Greek manuscripts, from the 10th or 11th century (Gray) to the 15th, place it with the books credited to Solomon, usually between Wisdom and Sirach, or after the Psalter (Swete, Introduction; Swete, vol. 3). The oldest witness to its name is the table of contents of Codex Alexandrinus in the 400s, which lists it after the closing count of the biblical books (Gray). Eleven Greek manuscripts are known today (Atkinson). Ryle and James judged that it "attained only a very limited circulation" but "where it was read, it seems to have been read with respect."

The book had "passed out of sight and almost out of memory" until it was printed in 1626 by J. L. de la Cerda from a faulty copy of one manuscript (Gray). The editions of Ryle and James (1891), von Gebhardt (1895) and Swete made it part of the standard study of the period, and Rahlfs printed it at the end of the poetic books of his Septuaginta (1935).

provenance.h: What it builds on in the Hebrew Bible
provenance.b:
• The Psalter: its forms, its headings and Selah, its righteous and wicked, its curse psalms; above all the royal Psalms 2, 72 and 89 and God's oath to David (17:4–5; 2 Samuel 7:12–16).
  • Isaiah: the shoot of Jesse with the spirit of wisdom and the rod of his mouth (Isaiah 11:1–5; 17:27; 17:42), the herald of good news to Zion (Isaiah 52:7; 11:2), and the road home for the exiles (Isaiah 40:3–5; 11:5–7).
  • Ezekiel: the shepherd of David's line (Ezekiel 34:23; 17:45) and the mark on the foreheads of the faithful (Ezekiel 9:4; 15:8–10).
  • Deuteronomy and the prophets of judgment: the nation from far away sent to punish Israel's sin (8:16; Deuteronomy 28:49), and the pattern of sin, exile and return (9:1–2).

rejected_why.h: It was never in the Hebrew Bible
rejected_why.b: No Hebrew copy survives, and no Jewish source names the book: every ancient reference that Ryle and James collected is Christian, and Jongkind finds it "only within Christian transmission." The Westminster Confession and the other Protestant confessions accept as the Old Testament only the books of the Hebrew Bible, and the Psalms of Solomon are not even among the Apocrypha read beside them (Westminster Confession 1.2–1.3).

rejected_why.h: It stood only at the edge of the Greek Bible
rejected_why.b: In the preface to his volume 3 Swete printed it among "three collections" (with Enoch and the Odes) which, "if they cannot in strictness be said to belong to the Greek Old Testament, have some peculiar claims to a place at the close of the Alexandrian Bible"; of the Psalms of Solomon he adds that they are "not actually included in any uncial MS." but "at one time followed the New Testament in the Codex Alexandrinus." In his Introduction he calls the book "a partial exception" to the rule that such writings "were not admitted into collections of canonical books." In the table of contents of Codex Alexandrinus it comes after the sum of the books of the Old and New Testaments, as an extra (Swete, Introduction; Gray). Jongkind reads that placing as a sign that it was "not regarded as part of Scriptures." The other great early codices do not have it, and Swete thought this may reflect canon 59 of the Council of Laodicea (about AD 360), which forbids idiōtikous psalmous, private psalms, to be read in church. Gray thought that canon "may be directed" against these psalms but is not free of doubt; two later Byzantine canonists, Zonaras and Balsamon, applied it to psalms legomenoi tou Solōmontos, said to be Solomon's (Ryle and James).

rejected_why.h: The canon lists called it disputed, then apocryphal
rejected_why.b: The Pseudo-Athanasian Synopsis (probably 500s AD) lists psalmoi kai ōdē Solōmontos (Psalms and Ode of Solomon) among the disputed books (antilegomena) of the Old Testament, with four books of Maccabees and Susanna. The Stichometry of Nicephorus gives the Psalms and Odes of Solomon, with 2,100 lines, among the books that are disputed and not read in church. The list of the Sixty Books, which Gray finds attached to the Questions and Answers of Anastasius Sinaita (about 640–700), puts Psalmoi Solōmontos among the apocrypha, beside the Assumption of Moses and the Apocalypse of Elijah (Swete, Introduction; Gray). Ryle and James called it "the solitary instance of an Old Testament book, which from being merely ἀντιλεγόμενον became ἀπόκρυφον," from disputed to rejected.

The title ascribes the collection to Solomon (Atkinson), and the copies call it the Psalms of Solomon or, in three manuscripts, the Wisdom of Solomon (Jongkind); two Byzantine canonists knew such psalms as said to be Solomon's (Ryle and James). But the headings of single psalms are generally thought to be later than the psalms (Atkinson), and the psalms speak of Pompey's Rome, centuries after Solomon. The Catholic Encyclopedia says that the collection "makes no pretensions to authorship by Solomon, and therefore is not, strictly speaking, apocryphal. The name of the wise king became associated with it later and doubtless was the means of preserving it" (Reid). Toy finds it "uncertain when and why the psalms were ascribed to Solomon."

No church argues that the book should be in the Bible. The question readers face is how to use it: as a witness to Jewish hope beside the Gospels (the Catholic Encyclopedia's "value in illustrating the religious views ... of the Pharisees in the age of Our Lord," Reid), not as a source of doctrine.

cited_in.b: The angel promises that "The Lord God will hand him the throne of David his father" (Luke 1:32) and a kingdom without end (Luke 1:33). Psalm 17 prays God to raise up the son of David as king over Israel (17:23), resting on God's oath that David's kingdom would not fail (17:5). Both draw on 2 Samuel 7:12–16; there is no sign that Luke used the psalm. The link is a shared hope, and it shows how the angel's words would sound to devout Jews of the time.

Swete noted "interesting coincidences between the Greek phraseology of the Psalter and that of the Magnificat and other Lucan canticles," pointing to Ryle and James, whose table (pp. xci–xcii) sets the Magnificat beside the psalms phrase by phrase: among them God's mercy on those who fear him (Luke 1:50; 13:11), the arrogant brought down (Luke 1:52; 2:35; 17:8), the hungry filled (Luke 1:53; 5:10–12; 10:7) and Israel his servant (Luke 1:54; 12:7). Ryle and James also found "no trace of Christian influence" in the psalms' Messianic passages (Swete). Both writings use the Greek of the Psalter and the prophets; no borrowing is claimed.

The angels call the newborn child christos kyrios, which this site renders "He is Messiah and Lord" (Luke 2:11). The same two words, without the article, describe the coming king in 17:36 as all the manuscripts have it, and in the Greek of Lamentations 4:20. Several scholars think that in the psalm they first meant "the Lord's Messiah" (Rahlfs, after Carrière; Atkinson; Toy). Luke did not need the psalm for the phrase, but it shows that the words were already joined in Jewish hope for the king.

Simeon waits for Israel's comfort and is promised that he will see "the Lord's Messiah" (Luke 2:26). The heading of Psalm 18 and 18:8 use the same genitive phrase, and 18:7 says "Happy are those who live in those days!", the days when the Lord does good things for the generation to come. The psalms show that "the Lord's Messiah" was a living phrase for devout Jerusalem Jews like Simeon. No borrowing is claimed.

Matthew opens with "Jesus Christ, son of David" (Matthew 1:1), and the title recurs in the mouths of the sick and the crowds (Matthew 9:27; Matthew 21:9). Psalm 17 already uses son of David as the name of the coming king (17:23), so it shows what the title meant to Jews of Matthew's time. The New Testament does not cite it.

Jesus asks "In what way do the scribes say the Messiah is David's son?" (Mark 12:35). The psalms show devout Jews two or three generations earlier already calling the coming king the son of David (17:23; 17:36). Toy calls the psalm's Messiah "a man without supernatural power" and Reid "merely human." Christians read Jesus' answer from Psalm 110 as pointing beyond a son of David who is only a man (Mark 12:36–37).

Christ will "shepherd them with an iron rod" (Revelation 19:15; compare Revelation 2:27 and Revelation 12:5). Psalm 17 gives the son of David the same rod of iron to smash the sinners like a potter's jars (17:26). Both come from Psalm 2:9, whose Greek has the same rod and the same potter's jars; the psalm shows that Jews before the New Testament already read Psalm 2:9 of the coming son of David. It is not a source for John.

"The Lord Jesus will do away with him by the breath of his mouth" (2 Thessalonians 2:8). The son of David destroys the lawless nations by the word of his mouth and strikes the earth with it (17:27; 17:39). Both rest on Isaiah 11:4, where the shoot of Jesse kills the wicked with "the breath of his lips"; the shared source, not the psalm, explains Paul's words.

An angel seals "the slaves of our God on their foreheads" (Revelation 7:3; compare Revelation 9:4). Psalm 15 says God's sign is on the righteous for salvation (15:8) and the mark of destruction on the sinners' foreheads (15:10). Both build on Ezekiel 9:4, where a mark is put on the foreheads of those who grieve over Jerusalem's sins. A shared image, not borrowing.

Paul tells slaves not to serve "like people who want to please others" (Ephesians 6:6; Colossians 3:22), using the rare Greek word anthrōpareskoi. The heading of Psalm 4 and the psalm itself attack the anthrōpareskoi, hypocrites who act for show. The word is the same; the setting is different, and no dependence is claimed.

"By nature we are Jews, and not sinners from the Gentiles" (Galatians 2:15). The psalms show that usage: Gray notes that for these writers "alien nations are as such 'sinners'" (he cites 1:1 and 2:1–2), and the conqueror who batters down Jerusalem's walls is "the sinner" (2:1); the son of David will "drive the sinners out of the inheritance" and "destroy law-breaking nations" (17:26–27). Paul takes up the Jewish phrase in order to argue that Jews too are justified only through faith in Christ (Galatians 2:16).

The disciples ask, "Lord, is this the time you are giving the kingdom back to Israel?" (Acts 1:6). Psalm 17 hopes for exactly that: a son of David who gathers a holy people, judges the tribes and divides the land among them (17:28–31). The question shows that this hope was alive among Jesus' followers; Jesus answers by sending them to the end of the earth (Acts 1:8).

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to what devout Jews in Jerusalem believed and feared in the generation before Jesus, the Psalms of Solomon are of the first rank: they can be dated within a few decades, they come from Judea, and they show in their own words the hope for a son of David, the language of the devout and the sinners, God's discipline and mercy, and life after death. As a text they are fair but thin: a Greek translation of a lost Hebrew original, known from manuscripts copied a thousand years later, with some places corrupt. As history they are poetry, not chronicle, but their allusions fit Pompey's conquest and death closely. Measured against the 66 books, they share and sharpen the Bible's hope for David's son and its trust in God's justice and mercy; they go beyond the Hebrew Bible on the rising of the righteous; their Messiah is a holy man raised by God, not the Son who dies for sinners and rises; and their hard line between the devout and the sinners sits in tension with the Gospels' welcome of sinners.

sections.h: 1. A witness to Jewish hope before Jesus: very high
sections.b: Here no church disagrees. Few Jewish writings of the period can be placed so exactly: soon after 63 BC and 48 BC, in Jerusalem (Gray; Jongkind). The book shows a devout circle that kept the Law closely, prayed in the forms of the Psalter, took suffering as God's discipline, believed that the righteous would rise to eternal life (3:16), and waited for a king of David's line (17–18). Ryle and James, Gray, Toy and Reid read it as a window on the piety of the Pharisees; scholars who doubt that its writers were Pharisees still read it as the voice of a real Jewish group of the generation before Jesus (Jongkind). Its partisan tone is part of its value: it shows how bitter the quarrel over the Temple and the throne was (Gray).

Fairly, but thinly. The Hebrew is lost, and the Greek is a stiff translation with lines that make sense only as misread Hebrew (Gray; Toy; Atkinson). The Greek manuscripts are late: Swete's eight run from the 10th or 11th century (Gray) to 1419, and they descend from one lost archetype; the two main branches differ in over two hundred places, most of which do not change the sense (Gray, citing von Gebhardt). Atkinson finds "no major textual variants" in the three manuscripts found since Rahlfs. The Syriac adds a second line of evidence where it survives. The most important variant for Christian readers is at 17:36, where all the manuscripts have "the Lord Messiah" and many scholars think the original was "the Lord's Messiah"; the variant note there gives both. Swete's printed text follows one manuscript, r, closely, so its numbering and readings sometimes differ from Rahlfs's.

The book makes almost no historical claims of its own. It names no person but David, Abraham, Jacob and Israel, and no place but Jerusalem, Zion and Egypt. Its allusions fit what Josephus and Plutarch say of Pompey: the rulers who opened the gates, the battering ram, the slaughter, the captives sent west, the death in Egypt and the unburied body (Gray; Jongkind). Where the psalms and Josephus differ, the psalms stress the trampled altar and are silent on Pompey's entry into the Holy of Holies (Gray). The headings' claim "of Solomon" is not history: they are probably later than the psalms (Atkinson). No church holds the book as Scripture, so no church's teaching depends on how the headings or the allusions are read.

sections.h: 4. Agreement with the 66 books, point by point
sections.b:
• Matches: God is king forever (17:1; Psalm 145:13); he keeps his oath to David (17:5; Psalm 89:3–4); he disciplines those he loves as a father (10:1–2; Proverbs 3:11–12; Hebrews 12:5–11); he feeds every living thing (5:9–11; Psalm 145:15–16); the coming king is righteous, wise and filled with God's spirit (17:42; Isaiah 11:2) and does not trust in horses (17:37; Psalm 20:7).
  • Goes beyond: the plain hope that those who fear the Lord will rise to eternal life while the sinner falls and does not rise (3:13–16) goes beyond most of the Hebrew Bible. Daniel 12:2 speaks of some rising "to life without end" and some "to shame," and Isaiah 26:19 ("Your dead will live!") is read by many as bodily resurrection and by others as the nation's revival (see the note there); the psalm speaks of the sinners' ruin, not their rising. The mark of destruction on the sinners' foreheads (15:10) adds to Ezekiel 9:4's mark of rescue. The detailed program of the son of David (17:23–51) goes far beyond any single passage of the prophets.
  • Stands in tension: the Messiah drives out foreigners and sinners and lets no resident alien live among his people (17:26–31), while the prophets also hope for foreigners joining God's people (Isaiah 56:3–8) and Jesus welcomes sinners (Mark 2:15–17). The book sets the devout against the sinners, yet its righteous person also stumbles and falls (3:5), clears out wrongs done by slipping and atones for sins of ignorance (3:8–9), and is spared, his offenses wiped out by discipline (13:9), because "the mercy of the Lord is on the devout" (13:11). Set beside Paul's "No one is righteous. Not a single one." (Romans 3:10) and "no living person is in the right in your presence" (Psalm 143:2), the question is how far that righteousness rests on God's mercy. The words on the soul's free choice (9:7) and on storing up life by doing righteousness (9:9) are read by some as close to Deuteronomy 30:19 and Romans 2:6, by others as in tension with salvation by grace (Ephesians 2:8–9); see the notes there.
  • Christian readings: read from the New Testament, the psalm's son of David is a witness to the hope Jesus fulfilled, and also changed: Jesus is David's son and more than David's son (Mark 12:35–37), the Lord's Messiah who reigns by dying and rising (Romans 1:3–4).

how_to_read.b: Whatever your church, the Psalms of Solomon are not in your Bible. Read them as you would read a prayer book from Jesus' grandparents' generation: honest prayers of devout Jews in a time of disaster, which show what they hoped for, not a word from God to you.

how_to_read.h: Read them as prayers of a party in crisis
how_to_read.b: Remember who is speaking. The writers had lost the Temple to rulers they thought corrupt, and then saw Rome take it. Their "sinners" are often other Jews, and their curses are the words of people with no power (Gray). Read the anger as a lament, the way the Bible's own curse psalms are read, and notice how much of the book is quiet trust: God feeds the poor, hears the one who calls, and disciplines as a father (5; 6; 10).

how_to_read.h: Read Psalms 17 and 18 beside the Bible and the Gospels
how_to_read.b: Open Psalm 2, Psalm 72, Isaiah 11 and 2 Samuel 7 beside Psalm 17, and see how the writer wove them into one portrait. Then read Luke 1–2 and Mark 12:35–37. You will see why devout Jews hoped for a son of David who would drive out Rome, and why a crucified Messiah was so hard for them to accept (1 Corinthians 1:23).

This site numbers the verses as Swete does. Most books and websites use Rahlfs's numbers: their "Psalms of Solomon 17:21" is this site's 17:23, and their 17:32 is this site's 17:36 (see "Three ways of numbering").

how_to_read.h: Let the Bible be the measure
how_to_read.b: Where the psalms agree with the Bible, as they often do, they show how Scripture shaped Jewish prayer. Where they go beyond it, on the rising of the righteous or the program of the Messiah, read them as one group's hope. Where they pull against it, on the welcome of foreigners and sinners, let the prophets and the Gospels decide.
